In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ionic conductivity of the LDH materials is controlled by the water content in the interlayer, and the water content is controlled by the interlayer anions (CO 3 2 − or OH − ).

Mg–Al layered LDHs show high conductivity in a wide temperature range of 100–200 °C, and the conductivity of the OH-type sample is as high as that of liquid electrolyte at room temperature, while the CO 3 type shows the conductivity jump around 80 ° C, which should be due to the CO 3  ↔ OH interlayer reaction.

the conductivity of Mg–Aldouble hydroxides is very sensitive to the interlayer anionic species, and that the interlayer reaction of CO 3  ↔ OH plays a critical role in the conductivity of the Mg–Al LDHydroxides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Mg–Al LDHytes show high ionic conductivity at intermediate temperature (50–200 °C) under saturated humidity conditions, and they can be used as solid electrolyte for intermediate temperature fuel cell.
the conductivity of Mg– Al LDHs can be tuned by changing the interlayer anions and/or by controlling the interlayer water content.
the conductivity of LDHs depends on the interlayer structure and the hydration state, and the latter is strongly affected by the interlayer structure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Mg–Al LDs are a good candidate as a solid electrolyte for intermediate temperature fuel cell.
the conductivity of LDHs can be enhanced by the interlayer reaction with water vapor, i.e., the interlayer reaction is a key to the high ionic conductivity.
Mg–Al LDs can be used as an electrolyte in a fuel cell at 100–200 °C.
